channel.title: Project Syndicate
channel.description: Project Syndicate commentary, each entry with its lead image and photo credit, the summary, the full byline, the article text as the site serves it to any reader, and a clean link to the article. Most articles show only their opening paragraph before a registration or subscriber wall; the rest is not reproduced.

item.title: The Silver Lining of a Data-Center Slowdown
item.dc:creator: Raghuram G. Rajan
item.description: With leading AI labs under intense competitive pressure to keep advancing the frontier of the technology's capabilities, resistance to the build-out of computing resources is not such a bad thing. The more time we can buy, the greater our chances of maximizing the potential benefits and mitigating the risks.
item.content:encoded:

item.title: What Nvidia’s Crisis Reveals About the Chip War
item.dc:creator: Pinelopi Koujianou Goldberg
item.description: Export restrictions, like those depriving China of Nvidia’s most advanced chips, may buy time by curtailing a competitor's access to frontier capabilities made elsewhere. But in any technological conflict, policymakers must remember that slowing a rival is not the same as strengthening oneself.

Photo: Norbert Millauer/Getty Images

item.title: When Export Restraints Are the Lesser Evil
item.dc:creator: Shang-Jin Wei
item.description: Governments face pressure to protect domestic industries while preserving access to cheaper foreign goods. The recent EU-China car-export deal offers an uneasy compromise that protects European automakers while keeping Chinese cars available to consumers, making it preferable to prohibitive tariffs.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Costfoto/NurPhoto via Getty Images

The recent EU-China car-export deal offers an uneasy compromise that protects European automakers while keeping Chinese cars available to consumers, making it preferable to prohibitive tariffs.

item.title: The Trade Losses That Nobody Counts
item.dc:creator: Jun Du
item.description: While much of the United Kingdom’s post-Brexit debate has focused on the monetary value of lost trade with the European Union, the composition of UK-EU trade flows warrants closer attention. A sharp decline in the variety of products shipped to Europe suggests that the economic costs have been greater than many realize.

item.title: Nigeria’s Big Bet on Health Care
item.dc:creator: Bola Ahmed Tinubu
item.description: Nigeria’s dependence on imported medicines and medical equipment leaves families exposed to exchange-rate fluctuations and hospitals at the mercy of global supply chains. Expanding domestic manufacturing is essential to reducing the cost of treatment and ensuring that more Nigerians can access quality care.

item.title: What Should the Nvidia Board Do?
item.dc:creator: Dambisa Moyo
item.description: The proper role of any corporate board is to strike a careful balance between stakeholders. In Nvidia's case, the board will have to consider not just the current trading price, but also how its decisions will affect the landscape in which it operates, its employees, and its license to trade.
item.content:encoded:

item.title: The Roots of Macron’s Failure
item.dc:creator: Zaki Laïdi
item.description: Although French President Emmanuel Macron has certainly made mistakes, his troubled presidency is symptomatic of a deeper problem. In the end, he failed to build something truly enduring because he was seduced by the same monarchical impulse that is a recurring feature of French political culture.

item.title: Yalta in Shenzhen?
item.dc:creator: Richard Haass
item.description: In principle, the planned summit of the US, Russian, and Chinese presidents could usefully address what should be done to limit the proliferation of nuclear weapons, ensure that AI is more a force for good than harm, and end ongoing wars and prevent new ones. But principle is one thing; in practice, we are likely to see something else.

item.title: The Perverse Effects of the AI Investment Boom
item.dc:creator: Paola Subacchi
item.description: As big tech companies increasingly turn to debt markets to finance massive investments in AI data centers, they are competing for the same pools of capital as many governments. With interest rates already high and public demands for spending on the rise, the timing could hardly be worse for vulnerable economies.

item.title: Oceania’s Three Goals for COP31
item.dc:creator: Tina Stege
item.description: To make COP31 the “Blue COP,” delegates must recommit to keeping the 1.5° Celsius warming goal alive, reform the climate-finance system, and address our dependence on the fossil fuels driving the ocean's warming and acidification. Pacific countries have long championed these causes, but now the rest of the world must join them.

item.title: Can Brexit Be Reversed?
item.dc:creator: Hugo Drochon
item.description: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called Brexit a mistake, and opinion polls show that his proposal to "go all the way" and rejoin the European Union has majority support. But Brexit was won by a movement, and only a movement can reverse it.

item.title: The Global Economy After the Iran War Ends
item.dc:creator: Dambisa Moyo
item.description: Even if the Iran war ended tomorrow, the global economy would not simply pick up where it left off. Reopening the Strait of Hormuz could bring down commodity prices and ease inflation, but postwar reconstruction could redirect capital away from the United States, undermining the AI supercycle and fueling de-dollarization.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Meysam Mirzadeh/Tasnim News/AFP via Getty Images

Even if the Iran war ended tomorrow, the global economy would not simply pick up where it left off. Reopening the Strait of Hormuz could bring down commodity prices and ease inflation, but postwar reconstruction could redirect capital away from the United States, undermining the AI supercycle and fueling de-dollarization.

item.title: Breaking Billionaires’ Political Grip
item.dc:creator: Maíra Martini
item.description: The US midterm elections showed that despite the outsize role of money in politics, even the biggest donors don’t always get their way. But defeating billionaires at the ballot box won’t stop them from buying political influence as long as the rules permit them to do so.

item.title: The Dance of Empires
item.dc:creator: Arnold Thackray
item.description: Empires have a habit of preparing to fight the last war while their rivals work out how to win the next one. The US is no different, pouring its resources into military adventures while China slowly but steadily reclaims the scientific and technological leadership that once made it the world's greatest power.

item.title: The Rare-Earth Game
item.dc:creator: Daniel Gros
item.description: China will probably not impose a rare-earth embargo, but it will keep the specter of one alive. And the West will probably not achieve self-sufficiency in this critical sector, but it will keep seeking to reduce its vulnerability to a supply shock through expensive capacity duplication and stockpiles.

item.title: Why Research Matters
item.dc:creator: Peter N. Miller
item.description: Over the past 21 months, in the country that has leveraged research to greatest effect, the government is slashing funding for it, closing centers where it is done, politicizing grant-making decisions, and bullying its single biggest engine: universities. The costs will be far greater than many realize.

item.title: Africa Needs a Different Kind of Climate Finance
item.dc:creator: Penelope Gregoriou
item.description: Roughly half of the climate finance that flows to Africa comes in the form of debt, with multilateral and bilateral development-finance institutions often lending at commercial rates to economies already struggling to carry the added costs. To maximize fiscal space, the instruments used to deliver climate finance need to change.

item.title: Effective Climate Action Requires Capable States
item.dc:creator: Mariana Mazzucato
item.description: With delegations from around the world gathering for another international climate conference, the question today is not whether governments should do more to address the climate crisis, but whether they even have the capabilities to do so. After 40 years of free-market orthodoxy, many simply do not.
